theme: A succession of unfaithful kings; Ahab and Jezebel
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 14:21-16:34. The narrative moves quickly through a series of kings in Judah and Israel. Notice the repeated formulas, and slow down at the arrival of Ahab and Jezebel.
settingTheScene: In the decades after the split, the books of Kings tell the story of both kingdoms side by side. The author uses a formula for each king: when he began to reign, how long he reigned, and a verdict on whether he did right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. In the south, Rehoboam, Abijam, and Asa reign. In the north, a succession of kings, with coups and civil war, leads to Omri and then to his son Ahab.
observation: Judah under Rehoboam did evil: they built high places, pillars, and Asherim, and there were male cult prostitutes in the land (14:22-24).
Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem and takes the treasures of the temple (14:25-26).
“For David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem” (15:4).
“Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done” (15:11).
Asa removes idols and his own mother’s position as queen mother, but “the high places were not taken away” (15:12-14).
Northern kings rise and fall: Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, each “walking in the way of Jeroboam” (15:25-16:28).
“Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him” (16:30).
He married Jezebel, daughter of the king of Sidon, “and went and served Baal and worshiped him” (16:31).
interpretation:
The summaries can seem repetitive, but the repetition teaches. In the north, king after king “walked in the way of Jeroboam.” No dynasty lasts. Baasha kills Nadab. Zimri kills Elah and reigns seven days before burning his own palace. Omri comes to power. The northern kingdom is unstable because it is built on a false foundation. Without the Davidic promise, it has no secure line.

In the south, the pattern is different. Even when kings are bad, there is a recurring phrase: “for David’s sake the LORD gave him a lamp in Jerusalem.” God’s faithfulness to the covenant with David continues. A lamp is a small light, but it does not go out. Judah’s survival, in spite of its unfaithful kings, is a sign of grace.

Asa stands out as a reformer. He removes idols and even deposes his grandmother for making an image of Asherah. It is a costly act of obedience. But his reform is incomplete, because the high places remain. And later, when threatened by Baasha, Asa will turn to a foreign king rather than to the LORD (2 Chronicles 16). Even the best kings have limits.

Chapter 16 introduces the worst. Ahab is described as doing evil “more than all who were before him.” The narrator says it was a “light thing” for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam. He went further and married Jezebel, a Sidonian princess devoted to Baal, and built a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria. The northern kingdom is now officially committed to a foreign god of storms and fertility.

The chapter ends with a detail that reaches back to Joshua. Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho “at the cost of Abiram his firstborn,” fulfilling Joshua’s curse. God’s word does not fail. The same word that brought the walls down still stands.
connection: Jesus is the Davidic king whose light is not a small lamp but the light of the world (John 8:12). Where the kings of Israel and Judah failed one after another, he is the one faithful king. Matthew 6:24 states that no one can serve two masters, a truth Ahab’s reign illustrated. 1 John 5:21 says, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”
application:
Ask what “high places” remain in your life, areas you have not fully surrendered.

Thank God for the lamp he keeps burning for his promises.

Consider how easily “light things” become heavy. What small compromise do you tolerate?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping a lamp burning for the sake of his promise.
Ask him to keep you from half-obedience and the high places you leave standing.
Ask him to help you serve him alone.
